prompts.title: Reading where a photoelectron peak sits
prompts.context: In the photoelectron spectra of sodium and magnesium, the 1s peak of sodium is at 104 MJ/mol and the 1s peak of magnesium is at 126 MJ/mol. Both 1s peaks have the same height.
prompts.prompt: Explain why the 1s peak of magnesium is at a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of sodium.
checklist: Says the position of a peak shows how much energy it takes to remove those electrons (binding energy), not how many electrons there are
Says the 1s electrons are in the first shell in both atoms, at a similar distance
Compares nuclear charge: 12 protons pull on magnesium's 1s electrons, 11 on sodium's

earns.answer: A peak's position is the energy needed to remove those electrons. The 1s electrons of both atoms are in the first shell, closest to the nucleus. Magnesium's nucleus has 12 protons and sodium's 11, so magnesium's 1s electrons are attracted more strongly and need more energy to remove.
earns.why: It separates what a peak's position means from what its height means, and compares the nuclear charge acting on electrons in the same shell.

misses.answer: Magnesium has two 3s electrons and sodium has only one, so magnesium's peaks are higher.
misses.why: It mixes up peak height (the number of electrons in a subshell) with peak position (binding energy). The number of 3s electrons does not explain the 1s binding energy.

prompts.title: Why magnesium holds its outer electron more tightly than sodium
prompts.context: First ionization energies: sodium (11 protons, [Ne] 3s¹) 496 kJ/mol; magnesium (12 protons, [Ne] 3s²) 738 kJ/mol.
prompts.prompt: Explain, using Coulomb's law, why the first ionization energy of magnesium is greater than that of sodium.
checklist: Says the electron removed is a 3s electron in both atoms, in the same shell, with the same 10 core electrons shielding it, so the distance from the nucleus is similar
Compares the nuclear charge of both atoms: 12 protons in Mg, 11 in Na
Links the larger attraction to more energy needed to remove the electron

earns.answer: In both atoms the electron removed is a 3s electron, in the third shell and shielded by the same 10 core electrons, so it is about the same distance from the nucleus. Magnesium's nucleus has 12 protons and sodium's has 11, so the Coulombic attraction on magnesium's 3s electron is stronger, and more energy is needed to remove it.
earns.why: It compares both atoms on both parts of Coulomb's law: charge (12 vs 11 protons) and distance (same shell, same shielding). Then it connects the stronger attraction to the larger energy.

misses.answer: Magnesium is smaller than sodium and has more electrons, so it holds on to them more tightly.
misses.why: "Smaller" is a result of the stronger pull, not its cause, and "more electrons" is not why the attraction is stronger. It never names the number of protons or the shell the electron is in.

prompts.title: Why potassium loses an electron more easily than sodium
prompts.context: First ionization energies: sodium (11 protons, [Ne] 3s¹) 496 kJ/mol; potassium (19 protons, [Ar] 4s¹) 419 kJ/mol.
prompts.prompt: Potassium has more protons than sodium, yet its first ionization energy is lower. Explain why.
checklist: Says potassium's valence electron is in the fourth shell, one shell farther from the nucleus than sodium's third-shell electron
Mentions the extra shielding from potassium's larger core (18 core electrons against 10)
Concludes the greater distance outweighs the extra protons, so the attraction is weaker and less energy is needed

earns.answer: Potassium's valence electron is in the fourth shell, while sodium's is in the third. It is farther from the nucleus and shielded by 18 core electrons instead of 10. Even though potassium has more protons, the greater distance makes the Coulombic attraction on that electron weaker, so less energy is needed to remove it.
earns.why: It deals with the apparent contradiction head-on: more protons, but a larger distance and more shielding, and it says which effect wins.

misses.answer: Potassium is heavier than sodium, so its outer electron is easier to knock off.
misses.why: Mass does not set ionization energy; Coulombic attraction does. The answer never mentions shells, distance or shielding.

prompts.title: Two ions with the same electrons, different sizes
prompts.context: Ionic radii: Na⁺ 102 pm; F⁻ 133 pm. Both ions have 10 electrons, arranged 1s² 2s² 2p⁶.
prompts.prompt: Explain why Na⁺ is smaller than F⁻, even though the two ions have the same number of electrons.
checklist: Says both ions have the same electron configuration, so the same number of occupied shells and the same shielding
Compares the nuclear charge: 11 protons in Na⁺, 9 in F⁻
Concludes the larger nuclear charge pulls the same electrons closer, making Na⁺ smaller

earns.answer: Na⁺ and F⁻ both have 10 electrons in the same two shells, so their shielding is the same. Na⁺ has 11 protons and F⁻ has 9, so the nucleus of Na⁺ attracts the same set of electrons more strongly and holds them closer, which makes the ion smaller.
earns.why: With the electrons identical, the only difference is the number of protons; the answer says so and connects it to size through the attraction.

misses.answer: Na⁺ is smaller because sodium lost an electron, and F⁻ is bigger because fluorine gained one.
misses.why: That describes how the ions formed, not why these two ions, which now have the same electrons, differ in size. It never compares the protons acting on those electrons.

prompts.title: Why the Cl–Cl bond is longer than the H–H bond
prompts.context: Bond lengths: H–H 74 pm; Cl–Cl 199 pm.
prompts.prompt: Explain why the Cl–Cl bond is much longer than the H–H bond.
checklist: Says the bonding electrons in Cl₂ are valence electrons in the third shell, while H uses its first-shell 1s electron
Says the larger atoms reach their lowest potential energy (where attraction and repulsion balance) at a larger distance between nuclei

earns.answer: Hydrogen shares its 1s electron, in the first shell, close to its nucleus. The electrons chlorine shares are in the third shell, much farther from its nucleus, so a chlorine atom is larger. The two Cl nuclei reach the distance of lowest potential energy, where attractions and repulsions balance, much farther apart than two H nuclei do.
earns.why: It explains length through the shell the bonding electrons occupy and the potential energy minimum, the model the course uses for bond length.

misses.answer: Cl₂ is much heavier than H₂, so its bond is longer.
misses.why: Mass does not set bond length. The answer gives no particle-level cause: no shells, no atomic size, no potential energy minimum.

prompts.title: Why magnesium oxide has a much larger lattice energy than sodium chloride
prompts.context: Lattice energies (the energy to separate one mole of an ionic solid into its gaseous ions): MgO about 3,800 kJ/mol; NaCl about 790 kJ/mol. Ionic radii: Mg²⁺ 72 pm, O²⁻ 140 pm, Na⁺ 102 pm, Cl⁻ 181 pm.
prompts.prompt: Explain, in terms of Coulombic attraction, why the lattice energy of MgO is much larger than that of NaCl.
checklist: Compares the charges of both ions in each compound: 2+ and 2− in MgO, 1+ and 1− in NaCl
Compares the distance between ion centers: the ions in MgO are smaller, so they are closer together
Links the stronger attraction to more energy needed to separate the ions, which is the lattice energy

earns.answer: In MgO the ions are Mg²⁺ and O²⁻, so the product of the charges is four times that of Na⁺ and Cl⁻. Both ions in MgO are also smaller, so their centers are closer (212 pm against 283 pm). Larger charges and a smaller distance give a much stronger Coulombic attraction between the ions in MgO, so far more energy is needed to pull them apart: its lattice energy is about five times that of NaCl.
earns.why: It names both ions' charges and both distances, which is what "both species" means for an ionic solid, and links the attraction to the energy needed to separate the ions.

misses.answer: MgO has the larger lattice energy because Mg²⁺ has a bigger charge than Na⁺.
misses.why: It looks at one ion only. The anion's charge (O²⁻ against Cl⁻) and the distance between the ions are left out, so the comparison is half made.

prompts.title: Why all three bonds in carbonate are the same
prompts.context: In the carbonate ion, CO₃²⁻, every C–O bond is 129 pm long. A typical C–O single bond is 143 pm and a C=O double bond is 123 pm.
prompts.prompt: Explain why all three C–O bonds in carbonate have the same length, between a single and a double bond.
checklist: Says carbonate has three equivalent resonance structures, each with the double bond to a different O
Says the real ion is one structure, an average of the three, with the electrons spread over all three bonds
Gives the bond order of about 1⅓, so the length falls between single and double

earns.answer: Carbonate can be drawn as three equivalent resonance structures, each with the double bond to a different oxygen. The real ion is not any one of them: the electrons of the double bond are spread over all three C–O bonds. Each bond has a bond order of about 1⅓, so all three are the same length, between a single (143 pm) and a double bond (123 pm).
earns.why: It treats resonance as a description of one real structure with delocalized electrons and uses bond order to explain the length.

misses.answer: The double bond keeps moving from one oxygen to the next very fast, so on average the three bonds look the same length.
misses.why: Resonance structures are not forms the ion flips between. The ion always has the same delocalized structure; nothing moves back and forth.

prompts.title: Polar bonds, but only one polar molecule
prompts.context: Electronegativities: C 2.55, S 2.58, O 3.44. CO₂ has no dipole moment; SO₂ has one.
prompts.prompt: Both CO₂ and SO₂ contain polar bonds. Explain why SO₂ is a polar molecule and CO₂ is not.
checklist: Gives the shape of each molecule from its electron domains: CO₂ linear (two domains, no lone pair on C); SO₂ bent (a lone pair on S)
Says the two equal bond dipoles cancel in the linear molecule but not in the bent one

earns.answer: Carbon in CO₂ has two electron domains and no lone pairs, so the molecule is linear and its two equal C=O bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel. Sulfur in SO₂ has a lone pair as well as its two bonds, so the molecule is bent; its two S–O bond dipoles do not cancel, leaving a net dipole.
earns.why: It reasons from electron domains to shape and from shape to whether the bond dipoles cancel, in both molecules.

misses.answer: SO₂ is polar because sulfur is less electronegative than oxygen. In CO₂, carbon and oxygen share electrons equally.
misses.why: The C=O bond is polar too (2.55 against 3.44). The difference between the molecules is their shape, which the answer never mentions.

prompts.title: Why iodine boils higher than chlorine
prompts.context: Boiling points: Cl₂ −34 °C (34 electrons); Br₂ 59 °C (70 electrons); I₂ 184 °C (106 electrons). All three are nonpolar.
prompts.prompt: Explain the trend in boiling points from Cl₂ to I₂ in terms of intermolecular forces.
checklist: Names the force: all three are nonpolar, so the only intermolecular forces are London dispersion forces
Gives the cause: more electrons and a larger electron cloud make the molecule more polarizable, so its temporary dipoles are larger
Says that boiling separates whole molecules (overcomes intermolecular forces); no covalent bond breaks

earns.answer: All three halogens are nonpolar, so the only forces between their molecules are London dispersion forces. Going from Cl₂ (34 electrons) to I₂ (106 electrons), the electron cloud is larger and more easily distorted (more polarizable), so the temporary dipoles are larger and the dispersion forces stronger. More energy is needed to separate the molecules from each other in the liquid, so the boiling point rises.
earns.why: It names the force in all three substances and explains its strength by electron count and polarizability, the reason the readers ask for.

misses.answer: I₂ has the largest molar mass, so it has the strongest bonds and the highest boiling point.
misses.why: Molar mass alone is not a reason, and "bonds" suggests covalent bonds break on boiling. It never names dispersion forces or polarizability.

prompts.title: Two liquids of nearly equal molar mass
prompts.context: Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH (46.07 g/mol), boils at 78 °C. Dimethyl ether, CH₃OCH₃ (46.07 g/mol), boils at −24 °C.
prompts.prompt: The two compounds have the same molar mass. Explain why ethanol boils about 100 °C higher than dimethyl ether.
checklist: Names the forces in both: both have dispersion forces and dipole-dipole forces; only ethanol has an H bonded to O
Says ethanol molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other (H on O of one molecule to a lone pair on O of another); dimethyl ether cannot, since its H atoms are bonded to C
Says the dispersion forces are similar (same atoms, same number of electrons), so the hydrogen bonds make the difference

earns.answer: Both molecules have the same atoms and electrons, so their dispersion forces are about the same, and both are polar. Only ethanol has an H atom bonded to O, so ethanol molecules hydrogen bond to each other; in dimethyl ether every H is bonded to C, so it cannot. The extra hydrogen bonding in ethanol takes more energy to overcome, so it boils higher.
earns.why: It names every force in both substances, rules out dispersion as the difference, and gives the structural reason one has hydrogen bonds.

misses.answer: Ethanol has hydrogen bonding because it contains hydrogen and oxygen.
misses.why: Dimethyl ether also contains H and O. Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded directly to N, O or F, and the answer never compares the two liquids.

prompts.title: Which liquid evaporates more readily
prompts.context: At 20 °C the vapor pressure of acetone, CH₃COCH₃, is 185 torr and that of water is 17.5 torr.
prompts.prompt: Explain at the particle level why acetone has a much higher vapor pressure than water at the same temperature.
checklist: Compares the intermolecular forces: water molecules hydrogen bond to each other; acetone (no H on O) has dipole-dipole and dispersion forces only
At the same temperature the molecules have the same distribution of kinetic energies, so a larger fraction of acetone molecules have enough energy to escape the weaker attractions
Connects more escaping molecules to a higher vapor pressure at equilibrium

earns.answer: Water molecules hydrogen bond to each other, while acetone has no H on its O and only has dipole-dipole and dispersion forces, which are weaker overall. At 20 °C a larger fraction of acetone molecules at the surface have enough kinetic energy to overcome the attractions and escape, so more molecules are in the vapor when evaporation and condensation balance. That gives acetone the higher vapor pressure.
earns.why: It compares both liquids' forces and links them to the fraction of molecules able to escape, which sets vapor pressure.

misses.answer: Acetone has a lower boiling point, so it has a higher vapor pressure.
misses.why: That restates the data instead of explaining it. Both properties come from the intermolecular forces, which the answer never compares.

prompts.title: Why a real gas falls short of the ideal pressure
prompts.context: At 500 K, 1.00 mol of NH₃ gas in a 1.00 L container exerts a measured pressure lower than the ideal gas law predicts.
prompts.prompt: Explain at the particle level why the measured pressure of NH₃ is lower than the ideal gas law predicts.
checklist: Says the ideal gas law assumes no attractions between gas particles
Says NH₃ molecules are polar and hydrogen bond, so they attract each other noticeably when crowded this closely
Says attractions pull molecules back as they approach the wall, so they hit the walls less often or with less force, lowering the pressure

earns.answer: The ideal gas law assumes gas particles do not attract each other. NH₃ molecules are polar and can hydrogen bond, and at 1.00 mol in 1.00 L they are close enough for these attractions to matter. A molecule about to hit the wall is pulled back by its neighbors, so collisions with the wall are less forceful and less frequent, and the measured pressure is lower than predicted.
earns.why: It names the ideal-gas assumption that fails, why it fails for this gas, and how that changes the wall collisions that make pressure.

misses.answer: Real gas molecules take up space, so the pressure is lower than ideal.
misses.why: The volume of the molecules makes the real pressure higher, not lower. A lower pressure comes from attractions, which the answer does not mention.

prompts.title: Which ion holds water molecules more tightly
prompts.context: In water, Li⁺ (radius 76 pm) and K⁺ (radius 138 pm) are each surrounded by water molecules.
prompts.prompt: Explain why water molecules are attracted more strongly to Li⁺ than to K⁺. Say how the water molecules are oriented around each ion.
checklist: Orientation: the partially negative O end of each water molecule points toward the cation
Same charge (1+) on both ions; Li⁺ is smaller, so the water's O can get closer to the center of the ion
Coulomb's law: the smaller distance gives a stronger ion-dipole attraction

earns.answer: Around each cation, the water molecules point their partially negative oxygen ends toward the ion. Li⁺ and K⁺ have the same charge, 1+, but Li⁺ is much smaller (76 pm against 138 pm), so the oxygen of each water molecule gets closer to the center of the ion. By Coulomb's law the shorter distance gives a stronger ion-dipole attraction for Li⁺.
earns.why: It gets the dipole orientation right and compares the two ions on charge and distance.

misses.answer: The hydrogen atoms of water point toward Li⁺ and form hydrogen bonds, which are stronger because lithium is small.
misses.why: The orientation is backwards (H points toward anions, O toward cations), and the attraction is ion-dipole, not hydrogen bonding.

prompts.title: What a fingerprint on the cuvette does
prompts.context: A student makes a calibration line from standards, then measures an unknown. Before measuring the unknown, the student leaves a fingerprint on the clear face of its cuvette, which absorbs some light.
prompts.prompt: Justify whether the student's calculated concentration of the unknown will be too high, too low or unaffected.
checklist: Says the fingerprint absorbs or scatters light, so the measured absorbance is higher than the solution's true absorbance
Uses A = εbc (or the calibration line): a higher absorbance gives a higher calculated concentration, so the result is too high

earns.answer: Too high. The fingerprint absorbs or scatters some of the light, so less light reaches the detector and the measured absorbance is higher than the solution's own. The concentration is read from the calibration line (A = εbc, with ε and b fixed), so a higher absorbance gives a calculated concentration that is too high.
earns.why: It states the direction, then traces the error through the measured quantity and the equation to the result.

misses.answer: The result will be inaccurate because the fingerprint interferes with the light.
misses.why: A justification of an error needs a direction (too high or too low) and the reason through A = εbc. "Inaccurate" earns nothing.

prompts.title: Why sodium and nitrate ions are left out
prompts.context: When solutions of AgNO₃ and NaCl are mixed, a white solid forms. The net ionic equation is Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s).
prompts.prompt: Justify why Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ do not appear in the net ionic equation.
checklist: Says Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are dissolved before mixing and stay dissolved, unchanged, after mixing (spectator ions)
Says only Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ change: they leave the solution to form the solid AgCl

earns.answer: Na⁺ and NO₃⁻ are separate, dissolved ions both before and after the solutions are mixed; they take no part in the change, so they are spectator ions. Only Ag⁺ and Cl⁻ change, leaving the solution to form solid AgCl, so only they appear in the net ionic equation.
earns.why: It says what each ion is doing before and after, which is the evidence for leaving it out.

misses.answer: NaNO₃ is soluble, so it is not written in the equation.
misses.why: It treats NaNO₃ as a product that forms, and does not say that its ions were present, unchanged, the whole time.

prompts.title: Boiling water is a physical change
prompts.context: Boiling 1 mol of water at 100 °C takes about 41 kJ. Breaking all the O–H bonds in 1 mol of water vapor takes about 926 kJ.
prompts.prompt: Justify the claim that boiling water is a physical change, using the energies given.
checklist: Says boiling overcomes the attractions between water molecules (hydrogen bonds and other intermolecular forces), so each H₂O molecule stays intact
Uses the data: the energy to boil (41 kJ/mol) is far smaller than the energy to break the covalent O–H bonds (926 kJ/mol), so boiling cannot be breaking those bonds
Says no new substance forms: the vapor is still H₂O

earns.answer: When water boils, the molecules separate from each other but each stays H₂O: only the intermolecular attractions (mainly hydrogen bonds) are overcome. The data support this: boiling takes about 41 kJ/mol, more than twenty times less than the 926 kJ/mol needed to break the O–H bonds. No new substance forms, so boiling is a physical change.
earns.why: It makes the claim, cites the two numbers as evidence and gives the particle-level reasoning.

misses.answer: Boiling is physical because the water can be condensed back into liquid.
misses.why: Some chemical changes can be undone too, so that is not the test. The answer ignores the energies and what happens to the molecules.

prompts.title: A buret rinsed only with water
prompts.context: A student titrates a measured volume of vinegar with standardized NaOH. The buret was rinsed with distilled water but not with the NaOH solution before it was filled.
prompts.prompt: Justify whether the calculated concentration of acetic acid in the vinegar will be too high, too low or unaffected.
checklist: Says water left in the buret dilutes the NaOH, so its real concentration is lower than the value used in the calculation
Says a larger volume of the diluted NaOH is needed to reach the end point
Concludes the calculated moles of NaOH (labeled molarity × larger volume) are too large, so the acid concentration is too high

earns.answer: Too high. The water left in the buret dilutes the NaOH, so it is less concentrated than its label. More volume is needed to deliver the moles of OH⁻ that react with the acid. The student multiplies the labeled molarity by this larger volume, which overstates the moles of NaOH, and therefore the moles and concentration of acetic acid.
earns.why: It follows the error through each quantity in the calculation to a direction, and names the correct practice implicitly (rinse with titrant).

misses.answer: The result is unaffected because water does not react with NaOH or with vinegar.
misses.why: Water does not react, but it changes the concentration of the NaOH in the buret, which the calculation assumes. The answer misses the dilution.

prompts.title: Why the rate law comes from data
prompts.context: For 2 NO₂(g) + F₂(g) → 2 NO₂F(g), initial-rate experiments give rate = k[NO₂][F₂].
prompts.prompt: A student predicted rate = k[NO₂]²[F₂] from the balanced equation. Explain why the student's prediction is not justified.
checklist: Says exponents in a rate law come from experiment, not from the coefficients of the overall equation
Says the overall reaction may go through several steps (a mechanism), and the slowest step sets the rate law
Uses the data: the measured rate is first order in NO₂, not second

earns.answer: The coefficients of an overall equation do not give the rate law, because the reaction need not happen in one step. The rate law depends on the steps the reaction actually goes through, especially the slowest one, and must be found from experiment. Here the data show the rate is first order in NO₂, not second, so the overall equation's coefficient of 2 does not appear as an exponent.
earns.why: It gives the reason the coefficients do not work (the reaction goes through steps, and the slowest sets the rate) and cites the measured order as evidence.

misses.answer: The student is wrong because the exponent for NO₂ should be 1.
misses.why: That restates the data. It does not say why coefficients cannot be used, which is what the question asks.

prompts.title: Which plot is a straight line
prompts.context: A student follows the decomposition of compound A and makes three plots of the data against time: [A], ln[A] and 1/[A]. Only the plot of 1/[A] against time is a straight line, with a positive slope of 0.45 M⁻¹ s⁻¹.
prompts.prompt: Determine the order of the reaction with respect to A and justify your answer.
checklist: Claims the reaction is second order with respect to A
Names the plot: 1/[A] against time is linear (and says the other two plots are not)
Links the linear plot to the order: 1/[A]t = 1/[A]0 + kt is the second-order integrated rate law, and the slope is k

earns.answer: The reaction is second order in A. The plot of 1/[A] against time is a straight line, while [A] against time and ln[A] against time are not. The second-order integrated rate law, 1/[A]t = 1/[A]0 + kt, is the equation of a straight line in 1/[A] against t, with slope k = 0.45 M⁻¹ s⁻¹.
earns.why: It names the linear plot, not just "the graph is linear", and ties it to the integrated rate law it comes from.

misses.answer: It is second order because the graph is linear.
misses.why: Three graphs were made, so "the graph" does not say which one. The readers give the point only when the linear plot (1/[A] against t) is named.

prompts.title: Why warming speeds a reaction
prompts.context: A reaction with an activation energy of 75 kJ/mol goes about three times faster at 35 °C than at 25 °C.
prompts.prompt: Explain, using the collision model, why the rate increases when the temperature is raised.
checklist: Says higher temperature raises the average kinetic energy of the molecules
Says a larger fraction of collisions now have energy at least equal to the activation energy (the main effect)
Says more effective collisions per second means a faster rate (collision frequency rises only slightly)

earns.answer: At the higher temperature the molecules have a higher average kinetic energy, so the energy distribution shifts and a larger fraction of collisions have at least 75 kJ/mol, the activation energy. More collisions each second are effective, so the reaction is faster. Molecules also collide a little more often, but that is a much smaller effect than the larger fraction with enough energy.
earns.why: It says why more collisions succeed (fraction above Ea), which is what explains a rate tripling for a 10 °C change.

misses.answer: At higher temperature the molecules move faster, so they collide more often and react faster.
misses.why: More frequent collisions alone cannot explain a threefold rise; the answer leaves out the activation energy and the fraction of collisions with enough energy.

prompts.title: Catalyst or intermediate
prompts.context:
A proposed mechanism for the decomposition of ozone:

Step 1: O₃ + Cl → ClO + O₂
Step 2: ClO + O → Cl + O₂

Overall: O₃ + O → 2 O₂
prompts.prompt: Identify the catalyst and the intermediate in this mechanism, and justify each choice.
checklist: Cl is the catalyst: it is used up in step 1 and made again in step 2, so it is present at the start and the end and is not in the overall equation
ClO is the intermediate: it is made in step 1 and used up in step 2, so it is not present at the start or the end
Distinguishes the two by the order: catalyst consumed then regenerated; intermediate formed then consumed

earns.answer: Cl is the catalyst: it is consumed in step 1 and regenerated in step 2, so the same amount is there at the end as at the start, and it does not appear in the overall equation. ClO is the intermediate: it is produced in step 1 and consumed in step 2, so it exists only partway through the reaction and also does not appear in the overall equation.
earns.why: Both species cancel from the overall equation, so the answer uses the order of appearance to tell them apart, which is the point the readers look for.

misses.answer: Cl and ClO are both catalysts, because neither appears in the overall equation.
misses.why: Cancelling out of the overall equation is true of both a catalyst and an intermediate. The answer needs which one is there first (catalyst) and which forms first (intermediate).

prompts.title: Same heat, different temperature change
prompts.context: 1.00 kJ of energy is added to 100.0 g of copper (c = 0.385 J/(g·°C)) and, separately, to 100.0 g of water (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)). The copper warms by 26.0 °C; the water warms by 2.39 °C.
prompts.prompt: Explain why the same amount of energy raises the temperature of the copper much more than the water.
checklist: Distinguishes heat (energy transferred, the same 1.00 kJ for both) from temperature (a measure of average kinetic energy of the particles)
Uses q = mcΔT with the data: same q and m, so ΔT is inversely proportional to c; water's c is about 11 times copper's

Gives a particle-level reason: 100 g of water holds about 3.5 times as many particles as 100 g of copper (5.55 mol of molecules against 1.57 mol of atoms), and in water some of the energy also goes into rotations and into stretching hydrogen bonds, so less goes into the average kinetic energy that temperature measures

earns.answer: Both samples receive the same heat, 1.00 kJ, and have the same mass, so by q = mcΔT the temperature change is inversely proportional to the specific heat. Water's specific heat (4.18 J/(g·°C)) is about 11 times copper's (0.385), so its temperature rises about 11 times less: 2.39 °C against 26.0 °C. At the particle level, 100 g of water is about 5.55 mol of molecules but 100 g of copper is only 1.57 mol of atoms, so in water the energy is shared among about 3.5 times as many particles; water molecules also take up energy in rotations and in stretching their hydrogen bonds. Less energy per particle goes into the average kinetic energy that temperature measures.
earns.why: It keeps heat and temperature apart, uses the equation with the given numbers, and adds a particle-level reason.

misses.answer: Copper is a metal, so it conducts heat better and gets hotter.
misses.why: Conductivity changes how fast heat spreads, not how much the temperature rises for a given amount of energy. The answer never uses specific heat or q = mcΔT.

prompts.title: A calorimeter without a lid
prompts.context: A student measures the enthalpy of neutralization of HCl and NaOH in a foam cup. The cup has no lid, so some heat escapes to the room during the reaction.
prompts.prompt: Justify whether the magnitude of the calculated ΔH (in kJ/mol) will be larger than, smaller than or equal to the true value.
checklist: Says heat lost to the room makes the measured temperature rise of the solution smaller than it should be
Says q = mcΔT is then too small, so the magnitude of ΔH (q per mole) is smaller than the true value

earns.answer: Smaller. Some of the heat released by the reaction escapes to the room instead of warming the solution, so the measured ΔT is smaller than it should be. The calculated q = mcΔT is therefore too small, and dividing by the same moles gives a ΔH whose magnitude is smaller than the true value.
earns.why: It gives the direction and traces the error through ΔT and q to ΔH.

misses.answer: The heat that escapes makes the reaction release less energy.
misses.why: The reaction releases the same energy; less of it is measured. The answer also never says whether the calculated ΔH is too large or too small.

prompts.title: Why making HCl releases energy
prompts.context: H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2 HCl(g). Bond enthalpies (kJ/mol): H–H 436; Cl–Cl 242; H–Cl 431. Estimated ΔH = (436 + 242) − 2(431) = −184 kJ/mol.
prompts.prompt: Explain, in terms of bonds broken and formed, why this reaction is exothermic.
checklist: Says breaking bonds requires energy (436 + 242 = 678 kJ per mole of reaction) and forming bonds releases energy (2 × 431 = 862 kJ)
Says more energy is released forming the two H–Cl bonds than is absorbed breaking the H–H and Cl–Cl bonds, so ΔH is negative

earns.answer: Breaking one mole of H–H bonds and one mole of Cl–Cl bonds absorbs 436 + 242 = 678 kJ. Forming two moles of H–Cl bonds releases 2 × 431 = 862 kJ. More energy is released by the bonds formed than is absorbed by the bonds broken, so the reaction releases a net 184 kJ per mole of reaction and is exothermic.
earns.why: It says which step absorbs energy and which releases it, with the numbers, and compares them.

misses.answer: The reaction is exothermic because breaking the bonds in H₂ and Cl₂ releases energy.
misses.why: Breaking bonds always absorbs energy. Energy is released when bonds form, and the answer gets this backwards.

prompts.title: Adding a catalyst at equilibrium
prompts.context: A mixture of SO₂, O₂ and SO₃ is at equilibrium: 2 SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2 SO₃(g). A catalyst is added at constant temperature.
prompts.prompt: A student claims the catalyst will produce more SO₃. Justify whether the claim is correct.
checklist: Says the catalyst lowers the activation energy of both the forward and the reverse reaction, speeding both by the same factor
Says the concentrations do not change when the catalyst is added, so Q is still equal to K, and K is unchanged at constant temperature
Concludes there is no net change: the amount of SO₃ stays the same

earns.answer: The claim is wrong. A catalyst gives a lower-energy pathway for both the forward and reverse reactions, so both rates increase by the same factor and remain equal. Adding it changes no concentration, so Q still equals K, and K is unchanged at constant temperature. There is no net reaction, so the amount of SO₃ stays the same; a catalyst only helps a system reach equilibrium sooner.
earns.why: It uses both arguments: equal effect on both directions, and Q = K with K unchanged.

misses.answer: The catalyst speeds up the forward reaction, so more SO₃ forms.
misses.why: A catalyst speeds both directions. The claim the answer agrees with is the misconception the readers list.

prompts.title: Adding hydrogen to an equilibrium mixture
prompts.context: N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) ⇌ 2 NH₃(g) is at equilibrium in a rigid container at constant temperature. More H₂ is injected.
prompts.prompt: Justify the direction the net reaction goes after the H₂ is added, using Q and K.
checklist: Writes or describes Q = [NH₃]² / ([N₂][H₂]³) and says adding H₂ increases the denominator, so Q falls below K
Says K does not change, because the temperature does not change
Concludes that Q < K, so the net reaction goes forward (making NH₃) until Q = K again

earns.answer: Right after the H₂ is added, Q = [NH₃]²/([N₂][H₂]³) is smaller than K, because [H₂] in the denominator has increased. K stays the same because the temperature has not changed. Since Q < K, the net reaction goes forward, using N₂ and H₂ and forming NH₃, until Q rises to equal K.
earns.why: It compares Q with K, says why K is unchanged, and gives the direction that restores Q = K. That is the reasoning the readers reward.

misses.answer: Adding H₂ increases the rate of the forward reaction, so the equilibrium shifts right and K increases.
misses.why: Rate language alone does not earn the point, and K does not change with concentration; only temperature changes K. There is no comparison of Q with K.

prompts.title: Halving the volume of a gas equilibrium
prompts.context: N₂O₄(g) ⇌ 2 NO₂(g) is at equilibrium at constant temperature. The volume of the container is suddenly halved, which doubles every concentration.
prompts.prompt: Justify which way the net reaction goes after the volume is halved, using Q and K.
checklist: Writes Q = [NO₂]² / [N₂O₄] and says that doubling both concentrations multiplies Q by 2²/2 = 2, so Q > K
Says K is unchanged at constant temperature
Concludes Q > K, so the net reaction goes in reverse (toward N₂O₄, fewer gas molecules) until Q = K

earns.answer: Q = [NO₂]²/[N₂O₄]. Halving the volume doubles both concentrations, so the numerator becomes 4 times larger and the denominator 2 times larger: Q doubles and is now greater than K. K has not changed because the temperature is the same. Since Q > K, the net reaction goes in reverse, forming N₂O₄, until Q falls back to K.
earns.why: It shows why Q changes (the squared term) instead of only saying "fewer moles of gas", and compares Q with an unchanged K.

misses.answer: The pressure increases, so the reaction shifts to the side with fewer moles of gas to relieve the stress.
misses.why: The direction is right, but this is Le Châtelier's rule of thumb without the Q vs K argument the question asks for.

prompts.title: Less silver chloride dissolves in salt water
prompts.context: AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq), Ksp = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ at 25 °C. The molar solubility of AgCl is lower in 0.10 M NaCl than in pure water.
prompts.prompt: Explain, using Q and Ksp, why AgCl is less soluble in 0.10 M NaCl than in pure water.
checklist: Says the NaCl already supplies Cl⁻, so Q = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] reaches Ksp at a much lower [Ag⁺]
Says Ksp itself is unchanged at 25 °C
Concludes that less AgCl dissolves before Q = Ksp, so the molar solubility (equal to [Ag⁺] from AgCl) is lower

earns.answer: In 0.10 M NaCl, [Cl⁻] is already 0.10 M before any AgCl dissolves. AgCl dissolves only until Q = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻] equals Ksp, which is still 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ at 25 °C. With [Cl⁻] so large, Q reaches Ksp when [Ag⁺] is tiny (about 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M), far less than in pure water, so much less AgCl dissolves.
earns.why: It keeps Ksp constant and explains the lower solubility through Q reaching Ksp sooner, with a number to show the size of the effect.

misses.answer: The Cl⁻ from NaCl lowers the Ksp of AgCl, so less of it dissolves.
misses.why: Ksp depends only on temperature. Saying the common ion changes Ksp is the error the readers report every year.

prompts.title: What a small Ka tells you about the particles
prompts.context: 0.10 M acetic acid, CH₃COOH (Ka = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵), has pH 2.87. A 0.10 M solution of HCl, a strong acid, has pH 1.00.
prompts.prompt: Explain at the particle level why the acetic acid solution has a higher pH than the HCl solution of the same concentration.
checklist: Says HCl ionizes completely, so [H₃O⁺] = 0.10 M
Says acetic acid is weak: Ka ≪ 1, so at equilibrium most molecules stay as CH₃COOH; only about 1% are ionized
Concludes [H₃O⁺] is much lower (about 1.3 × 10⁻³ M), so the pH is higher

earns.answer: HCl ionizes completely in water, so a 0.10 M solution has [H₃O⁺] = 0.10 M and pH 1.00. Acetic acid is weak: its Ka, 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, is much less than 1, so at equilibrium most of it stays as CH₃COOH molecules and only about 1.3% ionizes. [H₃O⁺] is only about 1.3 × 10⁻³ M, so the pH is higher, 2.87.
earns.why: It describes what the solution contains (mostly un-ionized molecules) and uses the size of Ka as evidence, not just the word "weak".

misses.answer: Acetic acid has a higher pH because it is a weak acid and HCl is a strong acid.
misses.why: "Weak acid" restates the claim. The readers want what weak means for the particles: most molecules stay un-ionized because Ka is small.

prompts.title: Reading pKa from a titration curve
prompts.context: 25.00 mL of a weak acid HA is titrated with 0.100 M NaOH. The equivalence point is at 18.40 mL, where the pH is 8.85. At 9.20 mL of NaOH the pH is 4.62.
prompts.prompt: Determine the pKa of HA and justify your answer.
checklist: Identifies 9.20 mL as the half-equivalence point (half of 18.40 mL), not the equivalence point
Says half the HA has been converted to A⁻ there, so [HA] = [A⁻]
Uses Henderson-Hasselbalch (or Ka = [H₃O⁺][A⁻]/[HA]): when [A⁻]/[HA] = 1, log 1 = 0, so pH = pKa = 4.62

earns.answer: pKa = 4.62. 9.20 mL is half of the equivalence volume, 18.40 mL, so half of the HA has reacted to form A⁻ and [HA] = [A⁻]. In pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]) the log term is log 1 = 0, so the pH at this point, 4.62, equals the pKa.
earns.why: It picks the half-equivalence point, says why the ratio is 1 there, and shows that the log term vanishes.

misses.answer: pKa = 8.85, because at the equivalence point all the acid has reacted.
misses.why: That confuses equivalence with half-equivalence. At equivalence no HA is left; the pH there is set by A⁻ acting as a base.

prompts.title: Diluting a buffer
prompts.context: A buffer is 0.20 M CH₃COOH and 0.20 M CH₃COONa (pKa 4.74). A student dilutes it with an equal volume of water.
prompts.prompt: Justify whether the pH of the buffer changes on dilution.
checklist: Uses pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]): the pH depends on the ratio of the two concentrations
Says dilution halves both concentrations, so the ratio stays 1 and the pH stays 4.74
Notes that the buffer capacity (how much acid or base it can absorb) does fall, because there are fewer moles per liter

earns.answer: The pH stays at 4.74. In pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]), only the ratio of the concentrations matters. Adding an equal volume of water halves both [CH₃COO⁻] and [CH₃COOH], to 0.10 M each, so the ratio is still 1 and the log term is still 0. What does change is the buffer capacity: the diluted buffer can neutralize less added acid or base per liter.
earns.why: It reasons from the ratio, which is the idea the readers find missing, and separates pH from capacity.

misses.answer: Adding water lowers the concentration of the acid, so the pH rises.
misses.why: It looks at one species. The conjugate base is diluted by the same factor, so the ratio, and the pH, do not change.

prompts.title: An ammonia buffer and the right pKa
prompts.context: A buffer contains 0.30 M NH₃ and 0.30 M NH₄Cl. For NH₃, Kb = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ (pKb 4.74). Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴.
prompts.prompt: Determine the pH of the buffer and justify the pKa you use.
checklist: Identifies the weak acid as NH₄⁺ and its conjugate base as NH₃, so Henderson-Hasselbalch needs the pKa of NH₄⁺
Finds pKa = 14.00 − 4.74 = 9.26 (from pKa + pKb = pKw, or Ka = Kw/Kb = 5.6 × 10⁻¹⁰)

earns.answer: In this buffer the acid is NH₄⁺ and the base is NH₃, so the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation needs the pKa of NH₄⁺, not the pKb of NH₃. pKa = pKw − pKb = 14.00 − 4.74 = 9.26. pH = 9.26 + log(0.30/0.30) = 9.26.
earns.why: It identifies the conjugate acid and converts pKb to pKa before using the equation.

misses.answer: The buffer is basic, so I use pKb: pH = pKb + log(0.30/0.30) = 4.74.
misses.why: Putting Kb (or pKb) into Henderson-Hasselbalch gives a pH below 7 for a basic buffer. The equation needs the pKa of the conjugate acid, NH₄⁺.

prompts.title: The sign of ΔS for a decomposition
prompts.context: 2 NH₃(g) → N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g)
prompts.prompt: Predict the sign of ΔS° for this reaction and justify your prediction at the particle level.
checklist: Claims that ΔS° for the reaction is positive (an increase in entropy)
Counts gas particles: 2 mol of gas become 4 mol of gas
Says more gas particles can be arranged in more ways (more microstates), so matter and energy are more dispersed; does not rely on the word "disorder"

earns.answer: ΔS° is positive. Two moles of gas molecules become four moles of gas molecules. With more independent particles moving through the container, there are many more ways to arrange the particles and share out their energy (more microstates), so matter and energy are more dispersed in the products.
earns.why: It counts the gas particles on each side and explains entropy as dispersal and microstates.

misses.answer: ΔS is positive because the products are more disordered.
misses.why: "Disorder" is the word the readers say does not earn the point. The answer needs the particle-level reason: more gas particles, more ways to arrange them and their energy.

prompts.title: When does limestone decompose?
prompts.context: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g); ΔH° = +178.3 kJ/mol, ΔS° = +160.5 J/(mol·K). Assume they do not change with temperature.
prompts.prompt: Justify whether this reaction is thermodynamically favored at 298 K, and at what temperatures it becomes favored.
checklist: Uses ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° with ΔS° in kJ: 0.1605 kJ/(mol·K)
Both ΔH° and ΔS° are positive, so it becomes favored above T = ΔH°/ΔS° ≈ 1,110 K, where the TΔS° term outweighs ΔH°

earns.answer: At 298 K, ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = 178.3 kJ/mol − (298 K)(0.1605 kJ/(mol·K)) = +130.5 kJ/mol. ΔG° is positive, so the reaction is not thermodynamically favored at 298 K. Because ΔH° and ΔS° are both positive, ΔG° turns negative only when TΔS° is larger than ΔH°, which happens above T = 178.3/0.1605 ≈ 1,110 K.
earns.why: It converts J to kJ, shows the calculation, and reasons from the signs of ΔH° and ΔS° to the temperature range.

misses.answer: The reaction is endothermic, so it is never favored.
misses.why: An endothermic reaction can be favored if ΔS° is positive and T is high enough. The answer never uses ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°.

prompts.title: A cell with a negative potential
prompts.context: Zn²⁺ + 2 e⁻ → Zn, E° = −0.76 V. Cu²⁺ + 2 e⁻ → Cu, E° = +0.34 V. A student wants to plate zinc onto a copper strip: Cu(s) + Zn²⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + Zn(s).
prompts.prompt: Justify whether this reaction can run on its own as a galvanic cell, and what is needed to make it happen.
checklist: E°cell = −0.76 − 0.34 = −1.10 V for the reaction as written
A negative E°cell means ΔG° = −nFE° is positive, so the reaction is not thermodynamically favored and cannot run as a galvanic cell
It can be driven as an electrolytic cell by an external power source applying more than 1.10 V

earns.answer: For the reaction as written, Zn²⁺ is reduced (cathode) and Cu is oxidized (anode): E°cell = −0.76 V − 0.34 V = −1.10 V. A negative E°cell makes ΔG° = −nFE° positive, so the reaction is not thermodynamically favored and will not run on its own. It can be forced as an electrolytic cell by connecting a power supply that applies more than 1.10 V.
earns.why: It calculates E°cell for the reaction as written, links the sign to ΔG°, and names what an electrolytic cell needs.

misses.answer: E°cell = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V, so the reaction will run on its own.
misses.why: That is the reverse reaction (zinc dissolving and copper plating). The answer reversed the half-reactions instead of using the reaction asked about.

prompts.title: Why E° is not multiplied by 2
prompts.context: Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag, E° = +0.80 V. Cu²⁺ + 2 e⁻ → Cu, E° = +0.34 V. Overall: Cu(s) + 2 Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2 Ag(s).
prompts.prompt: Calculate E°cell and justify why the silver half-reaction's potential is not doubled even though its equation is.
checklist: E°cell = E°(cathode, Ag⁺/Ag) − E°(anode, Cu²⁺/Cu) = 0.80 − 0.34 = +0.46 V
Says E° is an intensive property: it is energy per unit charge (1 V = 1 J/C), which does not depend on how many electrons are transferred
Says the electron count enters only through ΔG° = −nFE° (n = 2 here), not through E°

earns.answer: E°cell = 0.80 V − 0.34 V = +0.46 V. A potential is energy per coulomb of charge (1 V = 1 J/C), so it does not depend on how many electrons move; it is intensive. Doubling the silver equation doubles the electrons and the energy, but not the energy per coulomb, so E° stays 0.80 V. The number of electrons appears in ΔG° = −nFE°, with n = 2.
earns.why: It gets the value and gives the reason E° is not scaled, pointing to where n does enter.

misses.answer: E°cell = 2(0.80) − 0.34 = 1.26 V, because the silver equation is multiplied by 2.
misses.why: Multiplying E° by a coefficient is the error the readers report every year. E° is intensive.

prompts.title: How much copper plates out
prompts.context: A current of 2.00 A passes through a Cu²⁺ solution for 965 s. F = 96,485 C/mol e⁻; Cu 63.55 g/mol.
prompts.prompt: Calculate the mass of copper deposited, showing how you use the electrons per copper atom.
checklist: Uses 2 mol e⁻ per mol Cu (Cu²⁺ + 2 e⁻ → Cu): 0.0100 mol Cu × 63.55 g/mol = 0.636 g

earns.answer: q = It = (2.00 A)(965 s) = 1,930 C. mol e⁻ = 1,930 C ÷ 96,485 C/mol e⁻ = 0.0200 mol e⁻. Each Cu²⁺ gains 2 electrons, so mol Cu = 0.0200 ÷ 2 = 0.0100 mol. Mass = 0.0100 mol × 63.55 g/mol = 0.636 g Cu.
earns.why: Every step carries its unit, and the electrons-per-atom ratio from the half-reaction is used explicitly.

misses.why: It treats moles of electrons as moles of copper. Each Cu²⁺ needs two electrons, so the moles of copper are half the moles of electrons.
